full_judgment:
A TM Afzal, J. : This appeal by defendants Nos. 2 and 3, following leave, arises out of judgment and order dated 16 August, 1990 passed by a Single Judge of the High Court Division, Dhaka in Civil Revision No. 837 of 1985 discharging the Rule and upholding the concurrent decree of the Courts below in Title Suit No.197 of 1977 . 

 2. Plaintiff-respondent No. 1 filed the aforesaid suit, originally numbered as Title Suit No. 68 of 1974 in the Third Court of the Subordinate Judge, Dhaka and on transfer to the Fourth Court renumbered as above praying for a declaration that the decree dated 20.9.72 passed in Title Suit No. 35 of 1971 by the Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka, in respect of the suit property is void and not binding on the plaintiff, that the kabala dated 23.2.73 obtained through court in Title Execution Case No. 32 of 1972 is null and void and that the sale deed dated 8.3.73 executed by defendant No. 1 (respondent No. 2) in favour of defendant No. 2 (appellant No. 1) is void and not binding on the plaintiff. 

 3. The case of the plaintiff, in substance, is that the suit property along with other properties originally belonged to 3(three) brothers, Nibaran Chandra Mitra, Abinash Chandra Mitra and Satish Chandra Mitra who acquired the same by purchase on 21.4.1914. The joint properties of three brothers were amicably partitioned and the suit property fell in the saham of Abinash Chandra Mitra who died leaving behind three sons, defendant Nos. 4-6 (respondents 3-5), the Mitras, who transferred the suit property to the plaintiff by a registered deed of exchange on 13.11.63 through their constituted Attorney Syed Amir Ali. The plaintiff has been in possession of the same on payment of all rents and taxes. The suit property was requisitioned by the erstwhile Province of East Pakistan and after transfer the name of the plaintiff was mutated and he was paid monthly compensation by the Government. But subsequently the Government stopped payment and as such the plaintiff had to me Title Suit No. 107 of 1973 against the Government. In the said suit defendant No. 2 of the instant suit impleaded herself as defendant No. 7 and filed a written statement claiming that defendants No. 4-6 entered into an agreement with defendant No. 1 to sell the suit property and defendant No. 1 obtained an ex parte decree for specific performance of contract in Title Suit No. 35 of 1971. The plaintiff alleged that the decree passed in Title Suit No. 35 of 1971 was obtained fraudulently by suppressing all processes etc. Defendant Nos. 4-6 left the country long ago and had been residing in India permanently and they did not enter into any agreement with defendant No.1. Defendant No. 1 created the deed of agreement by practising fraud and obtained the ex parte decree by the same means. Hence the decree dated 20.9.72 obtained by defendant No. 1 in the said suit was null and void and the subsequent kabala in execution of the said decree did not confer any title to defendant No. 1 and defendant No. 2 did not acquire any title by her alleged purchase from defendant No. 1. The said decree and the subsequent deeds cast a cloud on the title of the plaintiff and as such the plaintiff had to file the suit. 

 4. Defendant Nos. 1 and 2 contested the suit by filing a joint written statement denying the material allegations of the plaintiff. They alleged, inter alia, that Probhabati Mitra, widow of Abinash Chandra Mitra also inherited with her sons in the suit property, that defendant No. 1 had an agreement with them for purchasing the suit property, that he obtained the ex parte decree against the Mitras in accordance with law and got the sale deed executed and registered through court, that the alleged power of Attorney is a forged one, that defendants 4-6 did not exchange the suit property with any property of the plaintiff, that the plaintiff had no property at Murshidabad which was shown to have been exchanged with the suit property, that defendant No. 3 was in occupation of the suit property as an allottee of the Government before it was de-requisitioned and it is now being possessed by defendant No. 2 as lawful owner by purchase, and that the alleged deed of exchange was registered in Pabna although the Mitras had no property at Pabna nor the plaintiff had any property in India. 

 5. Defendant Nos. 8 and 9, the Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property and the Government also filed a written statement contending that the suit property was requisitioned in 1948 and the name of the plaintiff was mutated as owner in place of the Mitras, that defendant No. 3 was an allottee, that the suit property has since been derequisitioned and that the decree obtained by defendant No. 1 in Title Suit No. 35 of 1971 is null and void. 

 6. The suit was once decreed earlier. The defendant-appellants went in appeal, title Appeal No.103 of 1978, which was dismissed and then they took a revision, Civil Revision No.1065 of 1979, in which the Rule was made absolute by the High Court Division and an order of remand to the trial court was passed. The remand was felt necessary because the High Court Division observed that the question of title of the plaintiff was directly and substantially in issue in the suit and without deciding that issue the plaintiff could not be given any relief under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and that a decision on the issue of title would also decide her locus standi to file the suit. After remand the plaintiff amended her plaint and at the trial, besides five issues already framed, three additional issues were taken up for consideration which are as follows: 

 7.	 Has the plaintiff claimed title to the suit property? 

 8.	 Has the plaintiff locus standi to file the suit? 

 9.	 Is the ex parte decree in TS 35n 1 of the 3rd Court of Sub-Judge, Dhaka a fraudulent, void and did the consequent sale deed in favour of the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 confer any title to the said defendants? 

 7.	The learned Subordinate Judge 4th Court, Dhaka by his judgment dated 28 April, 1983 decreed the suit again upon deciding all the issues in favour of the plaintiff. The title of the plaintiff was clearly found and as to issue No. 8 above it was found that the impugned ex parte decree and the Kabalas in pursuance of the same were obtained by practising fraud upon the court and as such defendant Nos. 1 and 2 did not acquire any title on the basis of the said documents. 

 8.	The appellants took an appeal against the said decree, Title Appeal No. 145 of 1983, which was dismissed by the Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka by his judgment dated 10 November 1985. Thereafter they filed a revision, Civil Revision No. 837 of 1985, in which the impugned judgment and order were passed. 

 9.	One of the main contentions of the contesting defendants in the suit was that the plaintiff had not acquired any title to the suit property on the basis of the deed of Exchange dated 13.11.63 (Ext. 2) because she had no right, title, interest or possession over any portion of the alleged property of Murshidabad, West Bengal the ownership of which was alleged to have been transferred to the exchangees, i.e. the Mitras as mentioned in Ext.2 Since the plaintiff was not the owner of the Murshidabad property, there was no transfer of ownership in exchange and as such the document Ext. 2 was void. At the hearing of the suit defendant No.3 (husband of defendant No. 2) who examined himself as DW 1 proved certain documents procured from and certified by Notary Public in India which were admitted into evidence without any objection. The Additional District Judge, inter alia, observed that the said documents were not admissible as those were not authenticated by the Bangladesh Mission in India. During pendency of the revisional application the said documents were got authenticated and an application was filed under Order 41 rule 27 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for accepting the documents in deciding the revision case. 

 11.	The High Court Division upon making reference to Sec. 119 of the Transfer of Property Act which provides for the right of a party deprived of thing received in exchange observed that even if the plaintiff failed to prove her title to the Murshidabad property the deed of exchange cannot be said to be invalid and that it is not necessary to decide whether the plaintiff had title to those properties. Being of such view the High Court Division did not think it necessary to consider the aforesaid documents. 

 13. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Advocate for the appellants, referred to the definition of 'Exchange' in section 118 of the TP Act and submitted that in a valid exchange there must be a mutual transfer of ownership of the properties between the parties to the exchange and since in the present case the documents as referred to above prove that the plaintiff had no title to and ownership over the properties of Murshidabad which were allegedly given to the Mitras by her in exchange, there was no exchange in the eye of law and the deed of exchange Ext. 2 was void. The suit being one for declaration of title of the plaintiff she was bound to prove that there was a valid exchange. Mr. Ahmed submitted that the view taken by the High Court Division was not in keeping either with the law or with the requirement of the suit. Mr. Ahmed also submitted that the High Court Division erred in totally ignoring the aforesaid documents of the defendant-appellants which has caused a miscarriage of justice. 

 14. Mr. Nurul Huq, learned Advocate-on-Record for the plaintiff-respondent, submitted that the contesting defendants being strangers to the exchange, they had no locus standi to question the validity of the exchange when the exchangees, the Mitras, who were made parties to the suit did not come to deny the transaction. It was a sufficient proof that there was a valid exchange and no further proof of the plaintiffs title to the Indian property was necessary. 

 15. Mr. Huq submitted that in the facts and circumstances of the case the view taken by the High Court Division was fully justified and no error was committed by the learned judge in not considering the Khatians etc. produced by the defendants which the plaintiff had alleged to be wrong and forged. Nevertheless, the lower Appellate Court fully considered the said document and rejected them, he pointed out. The two courts below having concurrently found title of the plaintiff and it having been further found that the defendants' decree and subsequent kabalas were vitiated by fraud, the High Court Division committed no error in discharging the Rule upon the view taken, Mr. Huq finally submitted. 

 16. Section 118 of the TP Act defines "Exchange". It says when two persons mutually transfer the ownership of one thing for the ownership of another, neither thing or both things being money only, the transaction is called an "Exchange". An exchange is a mutual transfer between two persons of the ownership of properties, but either both the things should be money or neither of them should be money. Therefore, transfer of ownership is a pre-condition for a valid exchange. When there is a question of title to be decided on the basis of an exchange deed, the party claiming title must prove that he had ownership in the property exchanged which had been transferred under the exchange. How it will be proved or when it is said to have been proved different matter. A party to the exchange when deprived of the thing or any part of the thing received by him in exchange because of any defect in the title of the other party has his remedy under section 119. But that is not to say that a third party can never raise the question of title of a party to the exchange. For example, in the present case, the defendants claiming title to themselves of the disputed property were competent to question the plaintiffs exchange. Therefore, the learned Judge of the High Court Division was not quite right in observing that even if the plaintiff failed to prove her title to the Murshidabad property the exchange cannot be said to be invalid or that it is not necessary to decide whether the plaintiff had title to those properties. Notwithstanding the said observations, however, the learned Judge was particular to notice that the lower appellate Court observed that the Mitras were satisfied with the title and possession of the plaintiff in the Murshidabad property as asserted by PWs 1 and 2 and there was no evidence from the side of the defendants to controvert the aforesaid evidence of PW s 1 and 2 and that the Mitras though made parties to the suit not one of them raised any objection or contested the suit. 

 17. The learned Judge satisfied himself that the Court of fact has found that the plaintiffs' title to and ownership over the Indian property was proved satisfactorily. 

 19. The learned Additional District Judge besides considering the defendants evidence as to alleged lack of title of the plaintiff went on to say that PWs 1 and 2 clearly stated that the plaintiffs title deeds were handed over to the Mitras, that PW 2 clearly stated that the Mitras were satisfied with the title and possession of the plaintiff, that the Mitras did not raise any objection or contest the suit, that the Government also did not raise any objection with regard to the title of the plaintiff as to her Murshidabad property, that the exchanges of the respective properties were made by both the parties in compliance with section 118 of the TP Act, that the certified copy of the Mitras' exchange deed was referred to in Ext. 2 and submitted to the Registrar's office and that as such it is futile to say that the plaintiff had no properties at Murshidabad, After such findings, the High Court Division had very little to do in revision when the said findings could not be assailed legally. It was not essential for the High Court Division to review the defendants' aforesaid documents over again because the Additional District Judge gave good reasons for not relying upon them. We have, however, ourselves perused the documents at the instance of the appellants. The Khatians which have been produced are of a date which is fourteen years after the execution of the exchange deed. The information slips by themselves do not carry much probative value. The plaintiff denied the said documents alleging them to be false and forged. Considering the evidence and circumstances in their totality, the court of fact (Additional District Judge) found that it was futile to say that the plaintiff had no properties at Murshidabad. There is no good reason to think that the said finding was for any reason erroneous or untenable. Therefore, it cannot be said that the learned Judge of the High Court Division misdirected himself to an extent causing an error in the decision and/or resulting in a failure of justice.
